limitations: All122PDF pages text-reviewed;six contact sheets cover all pages and30selected full-page visual checks address major lists,regimens and high-risk claims. Text alone was not used to infer printed labels.
Cover PDF1unnumbered;PDF2–122 have printed numbers equal to PDF positions. Do not invent printed1or apply the previous books’ minus-one offset.
There are21body chapter sections butonly labels1–20:the source repeats Chapter20at114and118. CH21 is explicitly editorial for the second20. No source renumbering.

Medical supply ledger preserves79bullet occurrences and78parent records:the blood-pressure cuff repeats twice on page28and maps to one parent. Other repeated products across source contexts retain duplicate-group links;79is not79distinct purchases.

Seven vital-sign rows and13infectious-disease section records preserve the source’s values/regimens without approving them. Source page context retains original detail;substeps,numerical cells and dose components are not extra parent tasks.

Author/combat-doctor credentials were not authenticated. Printed Marcus H. Ward differs from file-metadata Ashton Pereira;this difference is recorded without inventing a cause. Copyright2026does not prove up-to-date medical content.

No complete medical protocol,drug dose,pediatric treatment,triage algorithm,invasive procedure,sterilization method or five-person household capability is marked verified. Verified labels apply only to narrow supported principles.

Not every disease’s geography,incubation,symptom frequency,mortality figure or historical product statement was independently adjudicated. Those remain source-derived/needs_review,not silently confirmed. No current Virginia outbreak forecast supplied.

AHA2025BLS and2024AHA/RedCross first aid are distinct publications. Infant technique and choking guidance reflect2025updates;numeric overlap with older advice does not certify a full resuscitation protocol.

Clinical evidence is scoped:malaria childhood endemic vaccination is not routine traveler vaccination;mefloquine pregnancy prophylaxis differs from other contraindications;RMSF doxycycline age guidance is indication-specific;Ebola approved treatment is species-specific.

Source caveats are preserved:cannot replace medical study,professional help when available,contaminated-closure warning,spinal movement exceptions,refreezing warning,chest-seal worsening/edge-lifting,medication limits and invasive-risk warnings. Caveats do not resolve conflicting unsafe instructions.
FDA insulin source initially attempted at an obsolete URL;the correct information-regarding URL was subsequently opened. No evidence record depends on an inaccessible page or unread full text.

Virginia Poison Center,VDH bite/rabies guidance and Virginia prescription law address relevant local constraints;no personalized legal opinion,drug stockpile,patient diagnosis or site assessment performed.

EPA/USGS were not added as token authorities:there is no specific air-cleaning,groundwater/aquifer or treatment-system design here needing their verification. CDC constrains the boiling-water claim;the family irrigation well remains unapproved for drinking.

Household context remains five people,no pets,public water/sewer and irrigation well. Ages,conditions,prescriptions,allergies,training and clinical access unknown;no quantity or readiness credit calculated.

record.title: 2024 First Aid Guidelines
record.finding: First aid is limited by training and must seek further care. Supports scene safety, consent, direct pressure and appropriate escalation. Addresses chest wounds, spinal motion restriction, burns, anaphylaxis, oxygen, snakebite and fractures; topic-specific constraints are not a complete household clinical protocol.

record.title: 2025 Adult Basic Life Support
record.finding: Activate emergency response, use CPR/AED promptly, avoid delay from lay pulse checks and blind finger sweeps. Adult compression rate100–120/min and depth at least5cm while avoiding more than6cm. Severe responsive-adult choking uses5back blows alternating5abdominal thrusts, with specified exceptions.

record.title: 2025 Pediatric Basic Life Support
record.finding: Age, size and responder context change CPR and choking care. Infant compression uses one-hand or two-thumb encircling technique on an appropriate support; not arbitrary back-in-hand compressions. Breaths matter in pediatric arrest and infants do not receive abdominal thrusts.

record.title: First Aid for Seizures
record.locator: How to help; when to call; what to avoid
record.finding: Protect from surrounding hazards, stay, time the seizure and seek help for specified emergencies. Do not restrain, put objects in the mouth or give food/drink until fully alert.

record.title: Stop the Bleed just-in-time guide
record.finding: The primary guide explicitly says not to loosen or remove a bleeding-control tourniquet while awaiting professional care. Application needs suitable equipment/technique and monitoring; not a periodic-release schedule.

record.title: First Aid for Poisoning,2024
record.finding: Do not give activated charcoal as routine swallowed-poison first aid. Identify substance, time and amount and obtain case-specific advice. Route-specific decontamination differs; unconsciousness, seizure or inability to breathe requires emergency services.

record.title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do’s and Don’ts
record.finding: Antibiotics treat selected bacterial infections, not viruses. Use only as prescribed; do not share, save leftovers or take another person’s prescription. Broad symptom lists do not select the right medicine.

record.title: Cholera outbreaks
record.finding: The household fallback when ORS packets unavailable is1litre safe water,6teaspoons sugar and half a teaspoon salt. Packets follow their actual directions. Rehydration begins during illness; severe diarrhoea, inadequate intake, confusion or marked weakness need urgent care.

record.title: Personal Hygiene During an Emergency
record.finding: Handwashing and clean/covered wounds reduce contamination. Use appropriate safe water and obtain care for concerning infection signs. No surgical sterility or permission to probe deep wounds follows.

record.title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency
record.finding: Boiling/disinfection target germs, not all toxic chemicals, fuel or radioactive contamination. Match source and local advisory; cooled boiled water is not automatically sterile surgical fluid.

record.title: About Sepsis
record.finding: Sepsis is a life-threatening emergency. Without fast treatment, it can quickly cause tissue damage, organ failure and death. Home antibiotics and oral fluids do not establish a complete treatment plan.

record.title: Malaria vaccines:RTS,S and R21
record.finding: WHO recommends two malaria vaccines for children in malaria-endemic settings as part of comprehensive control. This contradicts no malaria vaccine exists, without making vaccination a routine Virginia family/traveler recommendation.

record.title: Yellow Book2026:Malaria
record.finding: Prophylaxis is destination/resistance/patient specific. Mefloquine can be recommended during pregnancy for chloroquine-resistant areas; psychiatric/seizure contraindications remain. Do not mix prevention and acute-treatment drug regimens.

record.title: Clinical Care of RMSF
record.finding: Doxycycline is first-line for suspected RMSF across ages, including young children and pregnancy under clinical care. Early treatment matters; other agents are not interchangeable just because the book lists them.

record.title: Treating Typhoid Fever and Paratyphoid Fever
record.finding: Timely appropriate antibiotics reduce complications/death. Untreated illness can persist weeks/months and become fatal; resistance can determine therapy. Do not wait for presumed self-cure.

record.title: Clinical Guidance for Ebola Disease
record.finding: FDA-approved treatments/vaccine exist for disease caused by Ebola virus, not all orthoebolaviruses. Suspected disease needs public-health notification, specific PPE/testing and professional care; not generic household symptomatic management.

record.title: Treatment of Low Blood Sugar
record.finding: Conscious patients who can swallow use appropriate fast carbohydrate and reassessment; young children may need different amounts. Severe episodes can need prescribed glucagon and emergency help. Oral glucose is not safe for an unconscious person.

record.title: Potassium Iodide in Radiation Emergencies
record.finding: KI has a narrow radioactive-iodine thyroid-protection role when officials/clinicians instruct. It does not protect against all radiation or establish treatment for an unexplained thyroid lump.

record.title: Frequently Asked Questions on Potassium Iodide
record.finding: Seafood/shellfish allergy does not necessarily imply iodine or KI hypersensitivity. KI indication, actual sensitivities and thyroid/other contraindications need medical/public-health assessment.

record.title: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings
record.finding: Normal adult BP is below120/80;140systolic or90diastolic is stage2hypertension, not a healthy default. Measurement, repeat assessment and symptoms matter; no blanket one-dose-until-normal plan follows.

record.title: Disinfection and Sterilization Recommendations
record.finding: Critical surgical instruments require validated sterilization, compatible equipment and process controls. Cleaning, disinfection, boiling/flame/alcohol improvisation are not interchangeable proof of surgical sterility. Healthcare guidance is applied as a limit, not a home operating-room design.

record.title: Code of Virginia54.1-3410
record.finding: Prescription dispensing has legal requirements and specific exceptions. Disaster language does not confer blanket permission to scavenge, possess or administer any prescription drug. Arrange lawful prescriber/pharmacy continuity.

record.title: Animal Bite
record.finding: Wash animal-bite wounds and seek proper medical attention; report exposures to local authorities/health departments for rabies assessment. Antibiotic ointment is not rabies prevention.

record.title: Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus
record.finding: Assess wound type and vaccination history for vaccine and, when indicated, tetanus immune globulin. Antibiotics are not recommended solely to prevent tetanus. Established tetanus requires medical treatment beyond a household antibiotic list.

record.title: About Bacterial Meningitis
record.finding: Meningitis involves the protective lining of brain/spinal cord; serious bacterial disease needs immediate medical evaluation/treatment. Transmission and contact prophylaxis depend on the cause and exposure, not every contact receiving an arbitrary antibiotic.

record.title: Eating,Diet and Nutrition for Kidney Stones
record.finding: Prevention depends on stone type and actual health conditions. Adequate dietary calcium can help prevent some stones; blanket dietary calcium restriction is not appropriate. Fluid advice must account for individual health.

record.title: Insulin Storage and Switching in an Emergency
record.finding: Follow actual insulin product storage and clinician instructions. Heat/freezing and product differences matter. Switching ideally needs medical supervision/close glucose monitoring; an unspecified hefty stockpile or symptom-based dose is not a plan.

record.title: Don’t Be Tempted to Use Expired Medicines
record.finding: Expiry and labeled storage matter; after expiry there is no guarantee of safety/effectiveness. FDA advises against expired use; government-controlled stability extensions do not establish a household medicine’s condition.

record.title: SALT Mass Casualty Triage Algorithm
record.finding: SALT separates immediate, delayed, minimal, expectant and dead categories with defined assessment/intervention/resource steps. An abbreviated color list or three priorities is not complete trained mass-casualty triage. Expectant and dead must not be conflated.

record.title: Using Alcohol to Relieve Your Pain
record.finding: Alcohol pain relief has harmful consequences and interactions: acetaminophen liver toxicity, aspirin gastric bleeding and opioid sedation/overdose risks. It is not a household emergency analgesic recommendation.

record.title: Garlic
record.finding: Raw topical garlic can cause irritation/chemical burns and oral/supplement forms can interact with medicines. It is not a validated interchangeable replacement for ibuprofen or wound treatment.

record.title: First aid:Act fast
record.finding: Do not induce vomiting. First aid depends on substance and route; contact poison specialists and emergency services for serious symptoms. Some caustic ingestions permit limited water/milk only when awake, not convulsing and able to swallow.

record.title: Foreign object in the skin:First aid
record.finding: Deeply embedded, very painful or concerning objects need prompt professional help; do not attempt deep removal. Padding around a significant embedded object can protect it without direct pressure on it.

record.title: A book is not clinical competence
record.guidance: Training, consent, scene safety, emergency activation and handoff remain essential. No collapse assumption authorizes every clinical intervention or proves no help exists.

record.title: Medicines require an actual patient plan
record.guidance: Check indication, age/weight, dose, allergy, pregnancy, interactions, renal/hepatic function, storage and monitoring. A supply list is not prescribing, permission or a complete kit for five people.

record.title: Assess without delaying life-saving care
record.guidance: Do not perform a long pulse search or head-to-toe diagnosis before indicated CPR/AED or hemorrhage control. Observe and communicate changes; single signs or normal vitals do not exclude serious injury.

record.title: Spinal care is not home manipulation
record.guidance: Minimize unnecessary movement and seek emergency care. Routine rigid collars/long boards are not recommended for general lay first aid. Do not rotate, force alignment or clear a spine by palpation; airway and immediate hazards may require movement.

record.title: Vital signs are context-dependent
record.guidance: The seven age rows are source reference values, not validated normal ranges or diagnostic cutoffs; BP omits diastolic values/units.140/90 is stage2hypertension rather than a healthy default. Do not auto-fill clinical thresholds from this table.

record.title: Triage needs a defined trained system
record.guidance: Do not equate a rough tag/priority list with a validated algorithm or label potentially living patients dead. SALT distinguishes expectant from dead; resources, assessment, interventions, reassessment and local incident command matter.

record.title: Airway and choking corrections
record.guidance: Do not perform blind finger sweeps, pin a tongue to a cheek or probe a throat with tweezers. Use age-appropriate current training/dispatcher guidance; severe responsive-adult choking uses5back blows/5abdominal thrusts with exceptions, and unresponsive choking moves to CPR. No tongue-swallowing myth or invasive airway improvisation approved.

record.title: CPR and ventilation need current context
record.guidance: Use2025age-appropriate CPR/AED training. Adult rate100–120/min and depth about5–6cm, with recoil/minimal interruptions; breaths only enough for visible rise.30:2is contextually appropriate, not universal for every infant/two-rescuer scenario. A surgical mask is not a rescue-breathing valve; do not press the abdomen to empty gastric air.

record.title: Shock,oxygen and positioning limits
record.guidance: Emergency care and control of the cause matter. No automatic5or10L/min oxygen, universal leg elevation or posture rule is endorsed. Oxygen requires suitable indication, equipment and training; oral fluids require adequate alertness/swallowing and appropriate injury context.

record.title: Bleeding control without timed release
record.guidance: Immediate direct pressure and appropriate limb tourniquets/wound packing can save life. Do not use neck/jugular pressure-point recipes or wait for a fixed loss volume. Do not periodically loosen/remove a tourniquet; professional conversion is different from a home timer. Page92’s later caution does not erase page58’s dangerous instruction.

record.title: Chest injuries need urgent professional care
record.guidance: No finger thoracostomy, needle decompression or anatomical insertion recipe is approved for lay use. An improvised three-sided seal is not a guaranteed one-way valve; occlusive dressings can worsen tension pneumothorax. Follow trained/dispatcher care and monitor/remove a dressing if breathing worsens as directed. Do not claim the book omits its page49burping/monitoring caveat.

record.title: Anaphylaxis is an emergency
record.guidance: Use the prescribed auto-injector/device instructions and call emergency services. Hold times vary; ten seconds is not universal. Antihistamines or heart-history guesses do not replace epinephrine assessment, and symptom improvement does not eliminate emergency evaluation.

record.title: Poison care is substance- and route-specific
record.guidance: Contact poison specialists promptly; do not induce vomiting or routinely give charcoal. A blanket nothing-by-mouth instruction is not correct for every exposure. Do not enter a toxic atmosphere to rescue without proper protection.

record.title: Seizure first-aid corrections
record.guidance: Do not restrain or place a bite block or other object in the mouth. Protect, time, stay and seek emergency help for prolonged/repeated/first seizures or breathing problems and other red flags. Food/drink waits until fully alert and safely swallowing.

record.title: Suspected clot or severe asthma is not a home drug sequence
record.guidance: Urgent professional assessment is needed. No generic aspirin+heparin+maintenance anticoagulant or oxygen+epinephrine+steroid sequence is approved. Bleeding risk, diagnosis, drug choice, contraindications and monitoring are missing.

record.title: Thermal injury scope and unsafe remedies
record.guidance: Burn depth/site/extent and age change urgency. Cool thermal burns promptly with clean water; AHA allows5–20minutes and monitor children for hypothermia. No large-blister lancing, hemostatic-gauze substitution, vinegar, witch-hazel, baking-soda bath or ordinary honey regimen for deep burns validated. Chemical/electrical burns need distinct care.

record.title: Cold and heat illness thresholds
record.guidance: Hypothermia is core temperature below35C/95F, not up to98.6F. Avoid direct heat/burn risks and rough handling; frostbite rewarming requires no refreezing risk. Heatstroke is an emergency requiring rapid cooling/EMS, not prolonged oral water treatment in impaired consciousness.

record.title: Wound assessment,closure and embedded objects
record.guidance: Clean superficial wounds appropriately and seek care for deep/contaminated wounds. Moving indoors does not make deep-object extraction, scalp glue/hair tying, suturing or duct-tape closure safe. Preserve source warnings against closing contaminated wounds without treating cleaning alone as clearance.

record.title: Bites and stings need exposure assessment
record.guidance: Animal/human bites need medical evaluation, rabies/tetanus assessment as indicated. Suspected venomous snakebite needs emergency care; North American pressure immobilization can harm and resting1–2days is not a substitute for antivenom. Skin appearance does not prove spider species; breathing/swallowing danger needs urgent help.

record.title: No untrained fracture/dislocation reduction
record.guidance: Do not pull, rock, worsen a deformity or forcibly reduce joints based on this book. Stabilize appropriately and assess urgently. Do not tightly bind broken ribs or jaws at the expense of breathing/vomiting safety. Splint checks are not permission to loosen a tourniquet.

record.title: Disease lists do not diagnose or prescribe
record.guidance: Symptoms overlap; tests, exposure history, local epidemiology, severity and clinician assessment determine treatment. Preserve each source regimen as research, not a ready prescription. Missing durations, maximums, allergies, pediatric/pregnancy/organ-function adjustments prevent operational use.

record.title: Malaria contradictions and pregnancy
record.guidance: Page13suggests malaria vaccination while page73says none exists. WHO malaria vaccines exist for specific endemic-childhood programs, not routine general Virginia vaccination. CDC permits mefloquine prophylaxis in pregnancy in appropriate destinations; the book’s blanket exclusion is wrong. Prevention is distinct from acute malaria treatment.

record.title: Meningitis is not merely respiratory disease
record.guidance: Inflammation involves brain/spinal-cord coverings. Bacterial disease is an emergency; arbitrary oral fallback antibiotics and blanket contact ciprofloxacin are not validated. Obtain urgent medical/public-health care.

record.title: RMSF treatment is time-critical and age-specific
record.guidance: Doxycycline is first-line across ages under medical care; do not substitute a generic tetracycline regimen or infer that young children cannot receive doxycycline for RMSF. Do not wait for a classic rash or delay for confirmation when clinical suspicion warrants treatment.

record.title: Typhoid and hemorrhagic-fever treatment claims
record.guidance: Do not wait for typhoid self-cure. Antibiotic resistance/severity determine treatment. No direct Ebola treatment is an outdated blanket claim: approved treatments exist for Ebola-virus disease, not all species. Suspected hemorrhagic fever requires specialized public-health/PPE care, not fear of migrants.

record.title: Diabetes emergencies and insulin continuity
record.guidance: Never put sugar in an unconscious patient’s mouth. Use the patient’s emergency plan/prescribed glucagon and emergency help. Do not choose IV fluids/insulin from symptoms alone; DKA requires monitored care. Insulin supplies need actual product storage/refill/switching plans.

record.title: Thyroid and KI corrections
record.guidance: An unexplained neck lump is not a diagnosis of iodine deficiency. KI is not a universal thyroid remedy; seafood allergy does not automatically equal KI allergy. Antithyroid and replacement medicines require diagnosis and monitoring rather than symptom-based substitution.

record.title: Blood pressure and aspirin are not universal remedies
record.guidance: 140/90 is not a healthy default. Do not treat until a number normalizes and then stop without a clinician plan. Chest-pain aspirin has alertness, nontraumatic-pain, allergy and prior-advice conditions; daily aspirin prevention requires individualized benefit/bleeding-risk assessment.

record.title: Kidney stones and urinary symptoms
record.guidance: Adequate dietary calcium is often beneficial; avoid blanket restriction. Stone type, obstruction, infection and patient fluid limits matter. Fever/flank pain or inability to urinate warrants prompt assessment; cranberry juice does not establish cure of kidney infection.

record.title: Tetanus prevention is not an antibiotic course
record.guidance: Rust itself is not the pathogen. Wound care and vaccination history determine vaccine/TIG prevention; antibiotics do not replace these. Suspected established tetanus needs emergency management beyond the listed drug doses.

record.title: Rehydration concentration and timing
record.guidance: Page85specifies no water volume, one teaspoon salt, potassium chloride and baking soda; do not use it as a recipe. Use labeled ORS or the accurately measured WHO fallback1litre/6level teaspoons sugar/half level teaspoon salt when appropriate. Begin rehydration during diarrhoea; do not wait for it to end or impose universal12-hour fasting. Oral fluids do not replace hemorrhage resuscitation.

record.title: Antibiotic stockpile labels are not prescribing
record.guidance: Amoxicillin, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole and azithromycin have different indications/resistance/adverse-effect constraints. A short purpose list or visible pus is not enough to select a regimen. Page105’s no-dosing statement conflicts with earlier explicit dose lists.

record.title: Medication storage and expiry
record.guidance: Follow each product’s actual label, including cold chain; cool/dry is not adequate for every medicine. Keep identity/instructions/expiry available, secure from children and plan lawful refills. Do not infer safety after expiry from appearance or a general may-remain-usable sentence.

record.title: Pain support without alcohol substitution
record.guidance: Comfort, appropriate support and calm communication can help, without proving stabilization is always the best analgesic. Do not give alcohol for emergency pain; interactions, bleeding, judgment and aspiration risks matter. Choose labeled medicines by the patient’s actual plan.

record.title: Clean is not sterile and no home invasive fallback
record.guidance: Boiling, flame and alcohol are not validated surgical reprocessing here. No home incision/drainage or invasive intervention is approved because help is assumed absent. The source’s own warnings about infection, bleeding and limits are preserved; they do not demonstrate safety.

record.title: Herbal substitutions are not equivalents
record.guidance: Garlic and raw honey do not become equivalent doses of ibuprofen or appropriate wound products. Raw garlic can burn skin; food use and laboratory activity do not validate this treatment.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
17 
Outback Medicine 
There is an interim scenario between first aid and survival medicine. 
Not every disaster occurs within a city or civilized region. Let’s say, 
for example, that you are involved in a plane crash and asked to 
provide aid for a fellow survivor, knowing that help could take hours, 
days or even weeks to arrive.  
Should you find yourself stranded far from civilization, you will 
become that patient’s best and perhaps only chance for survival. You 
will still need to administer first aid – diagnosing and providing 
immediate treatment for the problem – but you will als o need to 
factor in the follow-up care that will keep the person stable until help 
does arrive.  
Survival Medicine 
The third and final scenario assumes that help is not coming at all. 
This is a safe assumption in the case of a large scale disaster that cuts 
you off from civilization or leaves you as one of very few survivors.  
In this scenario, you are not just needed at the site of the initial injury. 
You will not only need to stabilize the injury and ensure the patient 
is given the best possible chances of a full recovery. After a collapse, 
you are that patient’s best chance of a full recovery and you will need 
to continue your care until the injury or illness is completely cured or 
controlled.  
This will also apply to conditions that are already present or that 
manifest after the disaster. You will need to be able to tackle chronic 
conditions such as arthritis, thyroid problems and heart disease as 
well as illnesses such as the flu and chicken pox.  
As will no doubt have become clear, survival medicine is an all -
encompassing skill with a different approach to basic first aid. For 
this reason, we will be covering both scenarios in this book to prepare 
you as fully as possible for what may come.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
19 
For any first responder to an illness, accident or injury, there is a basic 
order of duties that must always be followed. As the primary caregiver 
in a situation, whether it’s a car crash or a full collapse of civilization, 
it will be your job to provide that instant response and to do it in such 
a way that both you and your patient emerge in good condition.  
Because your safety and the safety of your patient are important and 
your aim is to make sure the person you are treating survives, this set 
of principles must become your mantra. Any and every time you are 
faced with a need to employ your skills, whether you are 
administering first aid until help arrives or you will be caring for the 
patient in the long term, these are the steps you must follow: 
1. Assess the situation. Cast a discerning eye over the scene you are 
faced with, looking for any dangers and hazards to either yourself 
or your patient. Ensure, for example, that you will not be hit by 
debris or injured yourself while trying to reach your patient. 
2. Remove immediate dangers.  Before you begin administering 
treatment, do everything in your power to prevent the situation 
from becoming worse. Your safety is as important as the patient’s 
– if you, too, are injured, their chances of survival are lost. 
Extinguish fires, remove loose debris and move your patient to a 
safer location if you cannot secure the scene itself. 
3. Protect yourself from contamination. As you do not yet know 
with full confidence what you are dealing with, make sure to 
protect yourself before you administer aid. A face mask, gloves and 
an apron are all important medical tools, not only to prevent 
contaminated fluids from contact with you , but also to protect 
your patient from contamination from your own body. 
4. Assess for threats to life. In that first instant, you do not need to 
know the full extent of your patient’s injuries. What you need to 
know first is whether any aspect of this situation will threaten the 
patient’s life. It’s no use diagnosing a compound fracture, for 
example, if your patient bleeds out in the meantime from a severed 
artery. You will need to check: 
5. Airway – is there anything blocking the person’s mouth or throat 
and preventing them from inhaling oxygen? 
6. Breathing – is the patient breathing normally? 
7. Circulation – is the patient’s heart still beating normally? Is there 
any bleeding severe enough to cause a threat to life?

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
20 
8. Extreme injury – has the patient suffered a neck or head injury 
that must be stabilized to ensure survival? 
9. Exposure – is the patient exposed to any external or 
environmental threat that could threaten their life?   
10. Treat life threatening issues.  Deal with any life threatening 
issues you have identified immediately, before continuing with 
your diagnosis and first aid. Ensure the patient is stabilized before 
you begin a deeper examination. 
11. Perform a thorough investigation. Your patient may or may not 
be able to communicate their injuries to you. If they are conscious, 
ask them to tell you what happened and where they hurt. This will 
provide you with at least some information to help your diagnosis 
but be aware that your pat ient may not be aware of every injury 
affecting them. Not all issues cause pain and some can cause 
numbness or paralysis. Examine the body thoroughly to be sure 
you are aware of less obvious issues and are able to provide initial 
treatment for them. 
12. Administer aid. Perform first aid on any wounds, breakages and 
other problems, such as shock and hypothermia. Your aim here is 
to stabilize the patient to give them the best chance possible of a 
recovery. Except in extreme conditions, the patient’s long term 
care will take place in a secondary location. 
13. Plan for evacuation. If help is on the way, your contribution may 
not reach this stage. If it is not, consider where and how you will 
transport the patient to a safe location and how you will prevent 
any part of their injuries from worsening in the process. 
14. Transport the patient.  Ensure that your patient is stable and 
secure before moving them. Particularly if there is a neck or back 
injury, moving the person can cause severe damage. You may need 
to consider creating a shelter where you are so that you can treat 
the patient in pla ce. If you feel that they are stable enough to be 
moved, make sure you have secured any broken limbs and that 
any bandages or wound coverings will stay in place.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
22 
All the while that you are following the guidelines we covered in the 
last chapter to successfully treat a patient at the scene of an accident 
or injury, there is a set of principles that any first aider should aim to 
follow. These principles strive to imp rove your chances of success – 
and to leave your patient in the best condition you can leave them in.  
Stay calm. Though not always an easy guideline to follow, this is 
imperative. You will make better decisions, notice more details and 
be more productive in a calm state of mind – when we hurry, we make 
considerably more mistakes. Not to mention the effect that your 
reaction will have on the patient – the last thing you want is an 
injured person panicking, attempting to move and in the process 
worsening their injuries and negatively affecting their own heart rate.  
Involve the patient.  As we briefly mentioned earlier, your patient 
knows better than you do exactly what happened to them, so their 
help can be invaluable. They can also tell you of hidden issues that 
could affect your treatment; for instance, perhaps they have a blood 
clotting disease that will increase the time it takes for a wound 
healing over on its own. Perhaps they feel nauseated or their head is 
throbbing – these are symptoms you cannot see, but that can help 
you reach an accurate diagnosis. Involving the patient has th e 
secondary outcome of keeping them calm and quelling their fears. It 
is only respectful, after all, to ask for permission before you begin 
treatment and to keep them appraised of your progress. No matter 
how good your intentions, remember that this is not  your body and 
you do not have an automatic right to touch it. 
Seek information. Whether or not your patient can communicate 
with you, there are still clues to their condition you can look for. 
Always assess the scene with an eye to causality: what exactly led to 
these injuries, and why? In many cases, this can lead to a better 
diagnosis or even allow you to spot more subtle injuries. It’s also a 
good idea to check for medical cards or bracelets that might alert you 
to pre-existing conditions. 
Assume the worst. Pessimism is not often thought of as a positive 
trait, but it’s certainly useful in a first aid situation. You may not be

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
23 
able to tell yet whether your patient is suffering from hidden injuries 
or a broken neck or back, so it’s always a good idea to assume that 
these problems are present. Better to go the extra mile to move a 
patient onto a stretcher than to discover too late , as you help them 
stand, that a neck injury was present all along. 
Enlist help. Speed can be of the essence in a crisis, both to ensure 
the patient’s survival and to complete your treatment and move the 
patient to a safer location as quickly as possible. Bystanders and your 
own companions may not be medically trained, but they can s till 
assist you in many of the tasks you will be called on to perform. In 
particular, it’s seldom a good idea to try to move a patient on your 
own unless you have no choice. 
Take charge. With that said, too many cooks have a habit of spoiling 
the broth. If you are enlisting help, be clear when you establish 
yourself as the medical authority in this situation. Announce that you 
are taking charge as a first responder and have the situation under 
control, using an authoritative tone. Request assistance and explain 
clearly what you need and why. Of course, it’s perfectly fine to 
relinquish your authority if you discover that there is a qualified 
medical professional within the grou p – deferring to greater 
knowledge and experience is never a bad idea. 
Consider all dangers . Accidents rarely happen in safe locations. 
Crashes, falls, even the disaster itself – all of these things have the 
potential to harm you and anyone else at the scene. Do not put 
yourself or anyone else in harm’s way without good reason. Throwing 
yourself in a churning river and being swept away to your own death 
will not save the victim and it is your responsibility and duty to make 
sure you do not endanger any bystanders or helpers by asking them 
to take on the danger for you. While treating the patient, continue to 
be alert for dangers and make sure your priority is to move everyone 
to a safer location. 
Think hard before you move your patient.  Only if a patient is in 
danger where they are or is recovered enough to be moved should

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
26 
As the person responsible for medicine and first aid within your 
group, you will also be responsible for ensuring that your shelter or 
kit bag is equipped for administering care. You are going to need 
plenty of supplies within your grasp and enough of those supplies to 
last for the amount of time you will be unable to obtain help from a 
hospital.   
In other words, if you are heading out on an excursion, you will need 
enough supplies to last for a few days, before help arrives. If you are 
stocking a shelter that will become a permanent residence after a 
collapse, you will need to be able to provide ai d for months, if not 
years.  
For everyday maladies and small problems, you will need:  
• Painkillers (and a child friendly version if you will have younger 
housemates)  
• Aspirin for aches, pains and heart problems  
• Benadryl for allergic reactions  
• Adrenaline injectors  
• Diarrhea medicine  
• Cough and sore throat medicine  
• Flu and severe cold remedies  
• Antibiotics  
• Women’s menstrual products (if you or your female companions 
are willing, you can purchase washable versions instead of 
disposable)  
• Diapers and baby care products  
• A good quality skin lotion  
• Stomach upset remedy  
• Antacids  
• Electrolyte replacement powder/ oral rehydration salts (for use 
after vomiting or diarrhea)  
• Calamine lotion  
• Burn spray or gel  
• Moleskin  
• Aloe vera gel for sunburn  
• Silver sulfadiazine cream  
• Potassium iodide tablets  
• Celox combat gauze

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
28 
For general equipment within your medical room:  
• A thermometer – preferably two, one oral and one rectal  
• A stethoscope  
• Latex or rubber gloves (if you opt for latex, be sure to check that 
none of your party is allergic to the material)  
• A surgical mask for use during first aid and surgery  
• Sterile gloves  
• Scalpels and scalpel blades of various sizes  
• A tourniquet  
• Syringes and injection needles  
• Sterilizing wipes to clean wounds  
• An airway  
• Tweezers  
• Scissors  
• A small flashlight, pen light or head lamp  
• A blood pressure cuff  
• Medical needle and thread for stitching wounds  
• Safety pins  
• Petroleum jelly  
• Cotton balls  
• A glucose meter  
• A blood pressure cuff  
• Bandages and dressings in every shape and size you are able to find  
• Compression wraps  
• A thermal blanket to treat hypothermia  
• Cold and hot compresses for swelling  
• Crutches and walking sticks to aid motion after a sprain, fracture 
or other injury  
• A stretcher.  
Though many of these items are easily found in pharmacies and even 
supermarkets, or can be ordered on the internet, you may find that 
you are unable to locate some of them. Do not worry: make it a 
priority after a disaster to locate a medical supply center . Find out 
now where the nearest one is to your shelter.  
You can both shore up your supplies and fill any gaps by doing this, 
often getting your hands on antibiotics and other medicines that are

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
31 
Never assume that you are seeing the full extent of the damage when 
you first encounter a patient. He or she may complain of nothing 
more serious than a bruised knee, but that doesn’t mean you are safe 
to assume that nothing else is wrong. After all, we’ve  all heard the 
stories of internal bleeding that went unnoticed until it was too late 
and the broken ankle that was walked on for two days before anyone 
noticed.  
A first responder should always aim to make an assessment of the 
patient’s full body, from head down to toe. Assume the worst – a 
criminal might be innocent until proven guilty, but a first responder 
knows that an injury is guilty until proven innocent.  
Your primary indicator of a patient’s status will be their vital signs: 
heart beat, breathing and blood pressure. As you begin your 
assessment of the situation, these are the details you will want to 
focus on.  
Vital signs, of course, vary according to the patient’s age. In general, 
look for vital signs in these ranges:  
• For a newborn baby, expect 30 to 50 breaths per minute, a pulse 
somewhere between 120 and 160 beats per minute and blood 
pressure of 60 to 80. 
• For a baby aged six months to a year , expect 30 to 40 breaths 
per minute, a pulse somewhere between 110 and 140 beats per 
minute and blood pressure of 70 to 80.  
For a toddler aged two to four, expect 20 to 30 breaths per minute, 
a pulse somewhere between 100 and 110 beats per minute and 
blood pressure of 80 to 95. 
• For a child aged five to eight years , expect 14 to 20 breaths per 
minute, a pulse somewhere between 90 and 100 beats per minute 
and blood pressure of 90 to 100. 
• For a child aged eight to 12 years , expect 12 to 20 breaths per 
minute, a pulse somewhere between 80 and 100 beats per minute 
and blood pressure of 100 to 110. 
• For a teenager aged 12 to 18 years , expect 12 to 20 breaths per 
minute, a pulse somewhere between 60 and 90 beats per minute 
and blood pressure of 100 to 120.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
32 
• For an adult, expect 12 to 18 breaths per minute, a pulse 
somewhere between 55 and 90 beats per minute and blood 
pressure of 120.  
Your initial examination of a patient needs to check off all the likely 
indicators of a problem. As a general rule, you can follow these steps 
to thoroughly investigate the person’s health and status:  
• Check for breathing. If your patient is not awake, place your ear 
near the nose and mouth to see if you can hear breath moving in 
and out. Watch their chest at the same time. Count the breaths 
according to the person’s vital signs. If the person is not breathing 
or is struggl ing to breathe, you will need to open the airway or 
breathe on their behalf. It is absolutely vital to steady the 
breathing first as your patient cannot go long without oxygen. If 
you hear noises such as a rattle in the breathing, there  may be an 
obstruction in the throat that will need to be removed. 
• Check the pulse. Use the tip of your middle and index fingers to 
check for a pulse on the artery at the patient’s wrist. If you cannot 
find one, check the inside of the upper arm (brachial artery), groin 
(femoral artery) or neck (carotid artery). If you are unable to find  
a pulse, you will need to administer chest compressions 
immediately. 
• Look for bleeding . Breathing and heartbeat should always be 
checked first for an unconscious patient, but a conscious one 
clearly has these functions to at least a good enough degree to be 
capable of speech. When dealing with a conscious patient, begin a 
dialogue with them as soon as possible to reassure them of your 
intentions and gather input from them. Meanwhile, look for 
bleeding. Any site of bleeding can be harmful, but heavy bleeding 
can be deadly very quickly. Examine the patient from head to toe 
to identify any areas of heavy bleeding. These must be addressed 
as soon as possible. 
• Perform a full body evaluation. Move clothing as much as you 
are able without unnecessarily exposing the patient. Look for 
obvious abnormalities anywhere on the body that could indicate 
fractures, wounds and other issues. 
• Check the patient’s mental status . If the patient is awake and 
speaking, you should ask questions such as name, profession, date 
and other facts to determine how lucid they are. Listen to the

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
33 
speech: if there is any abnormality, such as slurring, this could be 
a symptom of a problem such as hypothermia. 
• Check the blood pressure. The average blood pressure of a 
person at rest is 140/90. Too low may indicate shock or that your 
patient is hemorrhaging. 
• Feel the patient’s neck.  Gently check the vertebra and look for 
tenderness and muscles in spasm. Also check the Adam’s apple for 
a sensation almost like crunching. If you suspect any possibility of 
a neck injury, immobilize the neck as quickly as possible. Sudden 
movement can exa cerbate the problem and pain can cause a 
patient to twitch or try to move. 
• Check the spine. To look for back injuries, run your fingers down 
the spine, pressing gently to check for tender areas. Ask the 
patient to move their limbs and tell you if they have lost feeling in 
any areas. You can also pinch fingers and toes to check that the 
patient still has sensation. Any loss of feeling may indicate a back 
injury that will require the patient to be immobilized as securely 
as possible – and kept in one position unless necessary.

areas where the skull or skin is raised or depressed and look for 
any bleeding or abrasions. Shine a light into the patient’s eyes to 
check that the pupils are of equal size and respond to the light by 
constricting. If the pupils are small, this could be a sign of a brain 
injury or an overdose, while uneven pupils can mean the eye itself 
is injured or can also indicate head injury. Meanwhile, check for 
breaks and other problems on the head, suc h as a broken nose, 
loose teeth or a swollen tongue.

for a pale color that can indicate there is internal bleeding or 
anemia.

deformities and observe it to check that it is expanding and

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
32 
• For an adult, expect 12 to 18 breaths per minute, a pulse 
somewhere between 55 and 90 beats per minute and blood 
pressure of 120.  
Your initial examination of a patient needs to check off all the likely 
indicators of a problem. As a general rule, you can follow these steps 
to thoroughly investigate the person’s health and status:  
• Check for breathing. If your patient is not awake, place your ear 
near the nose and mouth to see if you can hear breath moving in 
and out. Watch their chest at the same time. Count the breaths 
according to the person’s vital signs. If the person is not breathing 
or is struggl ing to breathe, you will need to open the airway or 
breathe on their behalf. It is absolutely vital to steady the 
breathing first as your patient cannot go long without oxygen. If 
you hear noises such as a rattle in the breathing, there  may be an 
obstruction in the throat that will need to be removed. 
• Check the pulse. Use the tip of your middle and index fingers to 
check for a pulse on the artery at the patient’s wrist. If you cannot 
find one, check the inside of the upper arm (brachial artery), groin 
(femoral artery) or neck (carotid artery). If you are unable to find  
a pulse, you will need to administer chest compressions 
immediately. 
• Look for bleeding . Breathing and heartbeat should always be 
checked first for an unconscious patient, but a conscious one 
clearly has these functions to at least a good enough degree to be 
capable of speech. When dealing with a conscious patient, begin a 
dialogue with them as soon as possible to reassure them of your 
intentions and gather input from them. Meanwhile, look for 
bleeding. Any site of bleeding can be harmful, but heavy bleeding 
can be deadly very quickly. Examine the patient from head to toe 
to identify any areas of heavy bleeding. These must be addressed 
as soon as possible. 
• Perform a full body evaluation. Move clothing as much as you 
are able without unnecessarily exposing the patient. Look for 
obvious abnormalities anywhere on the body that could indicate 
fractures, wounds and other issues.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
34 
• Inspect the abdomen. Again, check for any cuts and wounds and 
press to see if there is any tenderness. 
• Check limbs and joints.  Press each arm and leg as well as the 
chest, ribs and collarbone to look for tenderness and breaks. 
• Take the patient’s temperature.  Abnormalities in a person’s 
core temperature can be a strong indicator that all is not well with 
the patient’s body. Too low may indicate a condition such as 
hypothermia, while too high may indicate hyperthermia or fever.  
These steps will allow you to evaluate the patient and check for 
symptoms of specific problems – more on these later in the book. If 
the patient is well enough to move, ask them to come with you to 
shelter and observe them for hours or days, depending on the severity 
of the injuries, to check for any deterioration and administer follow 
up care.  
Whether or not you need to keep the patient from moving, it’s best 
to always assume that the situation will deteriorate with time. Make 
sure to repeat your examinations regularly to look for new signs and 
signals and check that the symptoms you have identi fied have not 
worsened or spread.   
Also, you should continue to check the mental situation of the 
patient, to ensure that he or she remains lucid. Again, assume that 
the situation is likely to deteriorate with time. Try not to leave the 
patient alone unless absolutely necessary – if you must leave to fetch 
supplies or tend to a second victim, be sure to leave a volunteer to 
watch over them.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
36 
The best case scenario for an emergency responder who must work 
alone to help a patient is that you will only need to deal with the 
needs of one person. Unfortunately, especially in a survival situation, 
that won’t always be the case.  
That’s where triage comes in: a time honored practice used by 
medical professionals when they are overwhelmed by the sheer 
numbers of injured or sick people they must help as quickly as 
possible.  
In this scenario, follow these guidelines:  
Assess for safety. Earthquakes often have aftershocks. Damage to a 
building can mean delayed falling of debris. A disaster could cause a 
fire to spark. Never assume that you are safe to run in and begin 
helping your patients – and always assume that they will ultimately 
be better off if you are safe and whole. Many people have trouble with 
this concept – it can feel plain wrong to put your own safety above 
that of the injured. Remember that you are these people’s sole hope 
for medical attention and putting yourself in danger is very much 
against their interests. 
Assess the scene.  How many patients are you dealing with? What 
type of injuries are you seeing and how severe are they? Is there 
anyone else at the scene who might be able to help you? Is there an 
area nearby that you could use to gather the injured together?  
Ask for help.  If you have any form of communication device, 
summon help as quickly as possible. If you need someone to bring 
medical supplies for you, specify what you will need. If there are 
uninjured people on scene, ask for their help and ascertain how much 
medical training they have, which will dictate how they can assist 
you. Make it clear that you are in command of this situation – unless 
there is a more experienced medical professional nearby.  
Set up your treatment area.  Find the best possible place to bring 
patients together in one place after you have made sure they can 
safely be moved.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
40 
The first category of treatment we will look at deals with the injuries 
and issues that could threaten a person’s life. As a first responder, 
these are likely the techniques you will use first and foremost with a 
seriously injured patient.  
Clearing an Airway  
If your patient has vomited or their mouth and throat is blocked, they 
will be unable to breathe and will quickly become unconscious and 
then die. If your patient is unable to speak, appears panicked, has 
blue tinged skin or you can hear rasping and whistl ing as they 
breathe, gently lift the jaw forwards and upwards without moving the 
neck in case of injury. If there is no chance of a neck injury, place one 
hand under the person’s neck and the other on their forehead to 
gently tilt back the head, which will  open the airway as much as 
possible.   
Now, sweep two fingers in the patient’s mouth to check for any 
objects obstructing the breath. If the person is choking on their own 
tongue, you will need to pull it forward and out of the mouth and, in 
extreme circumstances, you may need to use a safety pin through the 
tongue and cheek to keep it from falling back down over the throat.  
If an object is lodged in the throat and cannot be grasped properly 
with your fingers without the danger of forcing it further down, use 
tweezers to remove it. If you cannot do this, sit the victim up and use 
your open palm to hit them on the back up to fo ur times firmly to 
dislodge the item.  
Heimlich Maneuver  
If your victim is choking and you are unable to retrieve the object 
with tweezers or slapping the back, you can also attempt the 
Heimlich maneuver if necessary. From behind the patient, clasp your 
hands around the upper abdomen, just below the ribs. Squeez e 
suddenly and very firmly then release. Do this two or three times to 
elicit a cough and ejection of the object in the throat. If this does not 
work, follow by slapping three to four times on the back and then 
repeat the Heimlich maneuver.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
40 
The first category of treatment we will look at deals with the injuries 
and issues that could threaten a person’s life. As a first responder, 
these are likely the techniques you will use first and foremost with a 
seriously injured patient.  
Clearing an Airway  
If your patient has vomited or their mouth and throat is blocked, they 
will be unable to breathe and will quickly become unconscious and 
then die. If your patient is unable to speak, appears panicked, has 
blue tinged skin or you can hear rasping and whistl ing as they 
breathe, gently lift the jaw forwards and upwards without moving the 
neck in case of injury. If there is no chance of a neck injury, place one 
hand under the person’s neck and the other on their forehead to 
gently tilt back the head, which will  open the airway as much as 
possible.   
Now, sweep two fingers in the patient’s mouth to check for any 
objects obstructing the breath. If the person is choking on their own 
tongue, you will need to pull it forward and out of the mouth and, in 
extreme circumstances, you may need to use a safety pin through the 
tongue and cheek to keep it from falling back down over the throat.

with your fingers without the danger of forcing it further down, use 
tweezers to remove it. If you cannot do this, sit the victim up and use 
your open palm to hit them on the back up to fo ur times firmly to 
dislodge the item.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
41 
If the patient cannot stand, sit astride their lower body and place your 
hands, one on top of the other, over the abdomen. Press down 
suddenly and firmly and then check the mouth to remove the object.  
If you are the person choking, it is possible to perform a Heimlich 
maneuver on yourself. Find a sturdy surface the height of your 
abdomen and throw yourself against it to produce the same reaction 
as your hands would on a patient.  
Mouth to Mouth Resuscitation   
If your patient is not breathing, you will need to do this for them – a 
lack of oxygen to the brain for any more than a couple of minutes will 
cause irreversible brain damage. Tilt the head backwards to open the 
airway, check the mouth for obstructions and  then pinch the nose 
closed with your fingers.  
Cover the patient’s mouth with your own (preferably while wearing a 
surgical mask for your own protection). Blow air into the person’s 
mouth until their chest rises – a full breath, which should take around 
two seconds. Remove your mouth from theirs to all ow them to 
exhale, then repeat.  
Be sure not to force the air into the lungs too hard, particularly with 
small children and babies. Repeat this cycle until help arrives or the 
patient begins breathing on their own. If you are encountering any 
difficulty blowing air into the lungs, this generally means there is an 
obstruction you will need to remove.  
In some circumstances, mouth to mouth resuscitation can cause the 
stomach to fill up with enough air that it becomes tense and hinders 
your efforts. If this occurs, turn the patient on their side and press on 
the abdomen. If this causes vomiting, clean out  their mouth before 
continuing.  
CPR  
If the patient has no heartbeat, you can pump the heart on their 
behalf. Kneel next to the patient’s chest and place your hands, one on 
top of the other, over the center of the patient’s breast bone. Interlock 
your fingers. The heel of your lower hand shou ld be approximately 
the width of two fingers above the bottom edge of the patient’s breast 
bone.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
42 
Line your shoulders up over your hands and keep your arms straight 
at the elbow. Keep your arms straight as you compress the breast 
bone around two inches and then release. You should be aiming for 
a speed that will provide around 100 compressions in one m inute. 
Regularly check for a pulse and breathing; if none is found, continue 
your efforts.  
For an infant, use one hand to hold the child’s back and the other to 
perform compressions. Your compression depth should be shallower 
at around 1.5 inches.  
Combining CPR and Mouth to Mouth  
In many cases, you will find that a patient without a heartbeat also is 
not breathing. In this scenario, perform 30 chest compressions and 
then administer two breaths using the mouth to mouth technique.   
Repeat this cycle until help arrives or the person begins breathing on 
their own. If you have a second helper, one person should administer 
the breath and the other administer the compressions to save 
switching time between the two techniques.  
Treating Shock  
Shock is a common reaction to a serious injury and is a condition you 
should keep a close eye out for as you treat that patient. If they do go 
into shock, it can be life threatening as the circulatory system is no 
longer providing sufficient oxygenated blo od to the patient’s body. 
This, in turn, leads to oxygen deprivation across the body.  
Watch for changes to the patient’s skin: it will likely become clammy 
and pale. The patient may sweat and exhibit shallow, fast breathing 
as well as feel weak, dizzy and nauseated. Watch for sighing and 
yawning as well as feelings of thirst.  
Lay the patient down and raise their legs into an elevated position 
(unless they have a severe head injury or a spinal injury). Cover them 
with a warm blanket and continue to speak to them reassuringly. 
Administer oxygen at a rate of 10 liters every minute  using a face 
mask.  
Recovery Position

and that your patient is breathing and has no other injuries that could

42 
Line your shoulders up over your hands and keep your arms straight 
at the elbow. Keep your arms straight as you compress the breast 
bone around two inches and then release. You should be aiming for 
a speed that will provide around 100 compressions in one m inute. 
Regularly check for a pulse and breathing; if none is found, continue 
your efforts.  
For an infant, use one hand to hold the child’s back and the other to 
perform compressions. Your compression depth should be shallower 
at around 1.5 inches.  
Combining CPR and Mouth to Mouth  
In many cases, you will find that a patient without a heartbeat also is 
not breathing. In this scenario, perform 30 chest compressions and 
then administer two breaths using the mouth to mouth technique.   
Repeat this cycle until help arrives or the person begins breathing on 
their own. If you have a second helper, one person should administer 
the breath and the other administer the compressions to save 
switching time between the two techniques.  
Treating Shock  
Shock is a common reaction to a serious injury and is a condition you 
should keep a close eye out for as you treat that patient. If they do go 
into shock, it can be life threatening as the circulatory system is no 
longer providing sufficient oxygenated blo od to the patient’s body. 
This, in turn, leads to oxygen deprivation across the body.

yawning as well as feelings of thirst.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
43 
prove life threatening, it’s usually a good idea to move them into the 
recovery position. This position makes sure that their airway stays 
clear because any vomit or other fluids that congregate in the mouth 
and throat can escape thanks to simple gravity.  
With the patient laying on their back, kneel beside them and place 
the arm closest to you at a right angle to their body, with the hand 
pointing up towards their head. Tuck the other hand beside their 
cheek on the same side and bend the knee furthest from you up and 
over so that it is across the leg that is closest to you. Roll the patient 
towards you by pulling the knee. If they are correctly positioned, their 
face should be supported by one hand and the knee and bottom arm 
will prevent them from rolling any further.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
45 
Serious injuries can be defined as the type of wound or injury that is 
either immediately a threat to the patient’s life or could become a 
threat if left too long without care. These are the injuries that you, as 
a medical care giver, should watch for duri ng that initial diagnosis 
after an accident or in the aftermath of a disaster.  
The most serious injuries should always be treated first, obviously. 
These techniques can mean the difference between life and death and 
will stabilize the patient, allowing you to begin diagnosing additional 
problems or treating other injuries.   
In some cases, these treatments are a first step only and you will need 
to revisit the wound later, once the patient has been moved to a safe 
place. Keep in mind that your goal is to save the patient’s life, so these 
first aid techniques are intended to st abilize injuries and prevent 
them from worsening.  
Gunshot Wounds  
Gunshot wounds are among the most dangerous injuries you may 
encounter in a crisis situation. 
They often appear smaller than they truly are. The visible wound may 
only tell part of the story, while the internal damage can be severe 
and life-threatening. For this reason, you should never assume that a 
gunshot wound is minor, even if the person is still conscious and able 
to speak. 
When assessing the injury, look for both an entry wound and an exit 
wound. The entry wound is usually smaller and more contained. The 
exit wound, if present, is often larger and more irregular, and may 
bleed more heavily. In some cases, there may be no exit wound, which 
means the projectile is still inside the body. 
Your first priority is to control bleeding. Apply firm, direct pressure 
to the wound using any clean material available. If the injury is on a 
limb and bleeding cannot be controlled with pressure alone, a 
tourniquet may be necessary. This should only be us ed when 
bleeding is severe and cannot be stopped by other means. 
Do not attempt to remove the bullet. The object may be limiting 
bleeding or preventing further damage. Removing it without proper 
conditions can make the situation worse.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
46 
If the wound is deep and bleeding heavily, apply steady pressure and, 
if possible, pack the wound carefully with clean material to help slow 
the bleeding. 
If the injury involves the chest, cover the wound as quickly as possible 
to prevent air from entering. This will help reduce the risk of the lung 
collapsing. You should refer to the section on chest wounds for more 
detailed guidance. 
Watch the person closely for signs that their condition is worsening. 
Weakness, confusion, or increasing pain may indicate internal 
bleeding, which cannot be treated easily in the field. In these cases, 
your goal is to keep the person still, calm, and stable. 
Once the bleeding is controlled, clean the wound as best as you can 
and apply a dressing to protect it from contamination. Infection is a 
serious risk with this type of injury, so care over the following hours 
and days is essential. If antibiotics are available and appropriate, they 
should be used to reduce the risk of infection. 
It is important to understand that you are not repairing the damage 
caused by the injury. Your role is to keep the person alive and prevent 
the situation from getting worse. 
Simple actions, done quickly and correctly, can make the difference 
between life and death. 
Protection of the Neck and Spine  
A neck or spinal injury can be deadly or, at the very least, cause 
permanent paralysis. A first responder must be conscious at all times 
of the possibility that such an injury exists. If there is a chance that 
the spine or neck has been broken or injured, immediately 
immobilize the patient’s head. Symptoms of this will include an 
inability to move the next or lower body, extreme pain or weakness 
and numbness and a loss of control of the bladder or bowels.  
Apply a sturdy neck collar. In the absence of this piece of equipment, 
place two rolled towels on either side of the head and use a wide 
bandage across the forehead to secure it. Use another towel around 
the neck to keep it from moving.  
If you need to align the head with the neck to secure it, be extremely 
careful with your movement and stop if you feel the slightest 
resistance. Rotate the head with both hands, starting by moving it so 
that the neck is not bent sideways without attempting  to rotate the

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
47 
head. If your patient is conscious, ask them to alert you to any pain 
or change in their condition as you do this. Be extremely careful not 
to flex the patient’s neck forward or backward as you move it.  
If the victim must be moved, either to a safer location or to allow 
them to vomit, grasp the shoulders while holding the head between 
your forearms as you do so. This will keep the head stabilized. You 
can use this method to move the patient onto a back bo ard or 
stretcher, allowing them to be transported safely without further 
movement of the spine.  
If your patient appears to have a spinal injury and you cannot slide a 
backboard underneath them, use the “logroll” technique. Have one

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
48 
slows, use a new dressing to firmly and tightly bandage the wound. If 
the wound continues to bleed or begins to bleed anew, do not remove 
the dressing. Apply pressure to stop the bleeding and then apply 
another pad and dressing over the top.  
Collapsed Lung  
If the patient has suffered an injury to the chest that has caused a 
puncture, this in turn creates an air leakage between the lung and the 
chest wall. The pleural space that resides here is usually full of 
negative pressure that allows the lung to compress and expand as we 
breathe. If you suspect this has occurred, use a stethoscope to listen 
to the breathing on both sides. One side will either feature 
diminished breathing sounds or no breathing at all.  
This is likely to be accompanied by other symptoms, such as a 
difficulty in breathing and pain in the chest area. The skin may turn 
blue and the veins in the neck may be distended, while the windpipe 
often shifts away to the side of the good lung.  
First, check for a chest wound and cover it immediately, as this could 
allow more air to enter the pleural space. Use a heavy dressing or tape 
to cover the wound. Air may accumulate in the pleural space under 
pressure, known as a pneumothorax, which will c ause the patient’s 
condition to worsen quickly and dramatically.   
If this occurs, push your finger through the wound into the chest to 
encourage the air to escape. The air will hiss as it does so and the lung 
will expand partially. This may save your patient’s life and will 
confirm your diagnosis of a collapsed lung.  
If there is no chest wound, you will need to allow the air to escape 
another way. Push a needle through the wall of the chest on the top 
side of the second to fourth rub, in the line directly down from the 
armpit. Seal the entry wound with a non-air permeable dressing and 
seal it only on three sides so that air can still escape, but cannot enter 
the wound.  
Now, administer oxygen through a tank at five liters per minute. Keep 
a close eye on the breathing rate and quality and assist with breathing 
if it becomes necessary.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
49 
Sealing Chest Wounds 
Injuries to the chest are especially dangerous because they can 
interfere directly with breathing. 
When the chest wall is punctured, air can enter the space around the 
lung instead of staying within the airway. This prevents the lung from 
expanding properly and can quickly become life -threatening if not 
addressed. 
A chest wound may produce a visible opening in the skin. In some 
cases, you may hear a sucking sound as the person breathes, or notice 
increasing difficulty in breathing. The person may appear distressed, 
breathe rapidly, or develop a bluish tint to the lips or skin as oxygen 
levels fall. 
Your first priority is to cover the wound as quickly as possible. 
Use any material that does not allow air to pass through, such as 
plastic, foil, or a similar smooth surface. Place it directly over the 
wound and secure it in place. If possible, fix it on three sides while 
leaving one side slightly open. 
This allows air to escape from the chest while reducing the amount 
of air that can enter. In effect, it helps prevent pressure from building 
inside the chest while still protecting the wound. 
Once the wound is covered, monitor the person closely. If their 
breathing becomes more difficult, or if their condition worsens, it 
may be necessary to briefly lift one side of the covering to allow 
trapped air to escape before sealing it again. 
Keep the person as still as possible and position them in a way that 
makes breathing easier, usually sitting slightly upright if they are 
conscious and able to maintain that position safely. 
Chest injuries can deteriorate quickly. Even if the person appears 
stable at first, their condition may worsen over time. Continue to 
observe their breathing, level of awareness, and overall condition. 
Your goal is not to fix the injury, but to prevent it from becoming 
immediately fatal and to support breathing for as long as possible. 
Anaphylactic Shock  
For a patient who has had an allergic reaction to a food or an insect 
bite, the symptoms can appear very quickly and can worsen rapidly,

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
49 
Sealing Chest Wounds 
Injuries to the chest are especially dangerous because they can 
interfere directly with breathing. 
When the chest wall is punctured, air can enter the space around the 
lung instead of staying within the airway. This prevents the lung from 
expanding properly and can quickly become life -threatening if not 
addressed. 
A chest wound may produce a visible opening in the skin. In some 
cases, you may hear a sucking sound as the person breathes, or notice 
increasing difficulty in breathing. The person may appear distressed, 
breathe rapidly, or develop a bluish tint to the lips or skin as oxygen 
levels fall. 
Your first priority is to cover the wound as quickly as possible. 
Use any material that does not allow air to pass through, such as 
plastic, foil, or a similar smooth surface. Place it directly over the 
wound and secure it in place. If possible, fix it on three sides while 
leaving one side slightly open. 
This allows air to escape from the chest while reducing the amount 
of air that can enter. In effect, it helps prevent pressure from building 
inside the chest while still protecting the wound. 
Once the wound is covered, monitor the person closely. If their 
breathing becomes more difficult, or if their condition worsens, it 
may be necessary to briefly lift one side of the covering to allow 
trapped air to escape before sealing it again. 
Keep the person as still as possible and position them in a way that 
makes breathing easier, usually sitting slightly upright if they are 
conscious and able to maintain that position safely. 
Chest injuries can deteriorate quickly. Even if the person appears 
stable at first, their condition may worsen over time. Continue to 
observe their breathing, level of awareness, and overall condition. 
Your goal is not to fix the injury, but to prevent it from becoming 
immediately fatal and to support breathing for as long as possible.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
50 
becoming life threatening in a matter of minutes. Symptoms may 
include itching and a raised rash, swollen extremities, eyes and lips, 
a feeling of faintness, swelling in the mouth, wheezing, nausea and 
collapse.  
First, ask the patient if they are carrying medication for the reaction 
– many people who have allergies severe enough to cause 
anaphylactic shock are aware of the condition and carry medication 
to treat it quickly, because there is often not enough time t o call 
emergency services even in a normal situation.  
Whether you can use the patient’s medication or must administer 
your own, the treatment is an adrenaline injection. Make sure to have 
some in stock and read the instructions carefully – preferably you 
should already have familiarized yourself with the tool . Once you 
have performed the injection, hold the syringe in place for ten 
seconds. The symptoms should begin to dissipate very quickly, 
though the patient should then rest on their back with their legs 
raised to encourage blood flow.  
Poison  
Poison comes in many forms and is especially likely in a survival 
scenario, where people may be relying on unfamiliar substances for 
food and can choose the wrong plant for their dinner. Most poison 
victims will vomit as their body automatically attempts t o reject the 
poison. They may also feel pain or a burning sensation and they may 
lose consciousness.  
Contrary to what may seem common sense, do not try to induce 
vomiting, though you can encourage them to spit out anything left in 
the mouth. Nor should you give the person any food or water to 
ingest. Instead, ask what the person has swallowed or whether t hey 
have inhaled poisonous fumes and keep a close eye on them in case 
they fall unconscious. If this happens, always place them in the 
recovery position in case of vomit. If the poison is on their clothing 
or skin, clean the area with warm water.   
A hospital or medical facility usually has antidotes on hand but, as 
this is likely not an option for you, your best bet is to use activated 
charcoal, which binds to the poison and prevents it from being 
absorbed into the patient’s bloodstream.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
51 
Be aware that activated charcoal can cause dehydration, so, after 
following the instructions carefully and allowing it to take effect and 
the patient to recover, you should make sure to encourage 
consumption of plenty of water.  
Burns and Scalds  
If your patient has been burned from fire, a hot surface or a chemical, 
your first step will be to stop the burning from occurring. You may 
need to douse them with water, smother them with a blanket or 
remove the patient from the vicinity of the material causing the burn.  
Next, remove any clothing or accessories that are close to the affected 
area of skin – unless it is stuck to that skin, because in this case you 
will cause additional damage. Cool the area with lukewarm running 
water for around 20 minutes, but keep the pat ient warm with 
blankets as you do so because there will always be a risk of 
hypothermia during this process. This cleaning process will also serve 
to wash out any chemicals or residue on the burn.  
Once the affected area is cooled, cover it with plastic wrap. You 
should aim to use it as a layer rather than a wrap. Treat the pain with 
painkillers.  
Electric Shock  
Be very aware of your own safety if a patient is suffering or has 
suffered an electric shock. The source is unlikely to deactivate by 
itself, so you will want to immediately find the source of the current 
and switch it off. In a survival situation, this ma y be a generator; if 
the power is still running, it could be the mains to the building the 
patient is in.  
The effects of the shock will depend on the voltage as well as how the 
current traveled through the patient’s body and their overall levels of 
health. Do not move the patient, but do apply a blanket to keep them 
warm and cover any burns with a sterile dressing. Make sure that you 
check for breathing and circulation, as a severe electric shock can 
cause the heart to stop. Perform CPR as quickly as possible.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
52 
Heart Attack  
Knowing the symptoms of a heart attack can save a patient’s life. If a 
person complains that they are suffering from chest pain, ask them 
where specifically the pain is and what it feels like. The pain of a heart 
attack is usually located in the center of the chest or the left side and 
feels like squeezing or pressure.  
The pain may also appear to be “traveling” around the body, usually 
down one arm or both arms or sometimes into the patient’s jaw, 
abdomen area or back.  
Sit the patient somewhere comfortable and give them an aspirin 
tablet of a 300 mg dosage. Ask if they have any history of heart 
problems and, if so, if they have the appropriate medicine with them 
or somewhere accessible. If the heart attack worsens, you m ay need 
to perform CPR to resolve a cardiac arrest.  
Seizures  
Your priority if a patient suffers from a seizure is to protect their 
ability to breathe – do your best to keep their airway clear if they 
vomit. Turn the patient onto their side and use a padded object as a 
bite block to prevent damage from involuntary biting actions.  
Try to prevent the patient from injuring themselves by using any 
available padding, such as a sleeping bag or cushion. Loosen their 
clothing and restrain them if necessary, making sure to keep them on 
their side.  
Most seizures stop within a couple of minutes, but the patient will 
suffer after effects including confusion and sometimes difficulty in 
breathing. As a second seizure may also sometimes follow, it’s 
important to watch the patient closely for at least an hour or so after.  
As and when the patient is able to communicate, ask whether they 
have a history of seizures and are taking any medication that should 
be administered. Ask if they are diabetic and, if so, give them a sugary 
drink or snack to regulate their blood sugar leve ls as an imbalance 
can sometimes be a cause of seizures.
