source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
110 
Pain is a natural response to injury. 
In an emergency, it can become a serious problem. Severe pain 
makes it harder for a person to stay calm, follow instructions, or 
remain still. It can also increase stress on the body and make the 
situation worse. 
Managing pain is not just about comfort. It helps improve control, 
stability, and recovery. 
Why Pain Control Matters 
When pain is high, people tend to move more, panic, or make poor 
decisions. 
This can lead to: 
• worsening an injury 
• increased bleeding 
• higher stress on the body 
Reducing pain helps the person stay still and makes it easier to 
manage the situation. 
Even small improvements in comfort can have a big effect. 
Start with Stabilization 
The first step in reducing pain is not medication. It is stabilizing the 
injury. 
If a limb is injured, keep it still. Movement increases pain and can 
cause further damage. 
Support the injured area using whatever is available. This could be a 
splint, a piece of wood, or even firm fabric. The goal is to prevent 
movement as much as possible. 
For general injuries, have the person lie down or sit in a stable 
position. Avoid unnecessary movement. 
Use Positioning to Reduce Pain 
The way a person is positioned can make a difference. 
In many cases: 
• keeping the body supported reduces strain 
• elevating certain areas can reduce pressure 
• avoiding awkward positions helps prevent additional pain

source_citations.section: Comfortable support and safe positioning / page context

source_components.source_label: Documentary page context; adjacent material may be included; image text is not transcribed here
source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
111 
Let the person settle into a position that feels stable and reduces 
discomfort, as long as it does not interfere with safety. 
Apply Cold or Heat Carefully 
Cold can help reduce swelling and numb pain, especially in the early 
stages of an injury. 
A cold compress, wrapped in cloth, can be applied for short periods. 
Do not place ice directly on the skin. 
Heat can help with muscle tension or stiffness, but it should not be 
used on fresh injuries that involve swelling. 
Use these methods carefully and observe how the person responds. 
Using Basic Medications 
If available, basic over-the-counter medications can help manage 
pain. 
These can reduce discomfort and allow the person to rest. They can 
also help reduce inflammation in some cases. 
Use only what you understand and have used safely before. In a 
crisis, it is important not to create new risks. 
Managing Severe Pain with Limited 
Options 
In some situations, pain may be far more intense than simple 
methods can control. 
Severe injuries such as fractures, burns, or deep wounds can cause 
extreme discomfort. When pain reaches this level, it can interfere 
with breathing, movement, and the person’s ability to remain calm. 
In a setting without access to strong medication, your approach 
must rely on control rather than elimination of pain. 
The most effective method is still stabilization. 
Keeping the injured area completely still reduces the body’s 
response to pain. Even small movements can make the situation 
worse, so supporting the injury properly is essential. A well-placed 
splint or firm support can significantly reduce discomfort.

Using Basic Medications 
If available, basic over-the-counter medications can help manage 
pain. 
These can reduce discomfort and allow the person to rest. They can 
also help reduce inflammation in some cases. 
Use only what you understand and have used safely before. In a 
crisis, it is important not to create new risks. 
Managing Severe Pain with Limited 
Options 
In some situations, pain may be far more intense than simple 
methods can control. 
Severe injuries such as fractures, burns, or deep wounds can cause 
extreme discomfort. When pain reaches this level, it can interfere 
with breathing, movement, and the person’s ability to remain calm. 
In a setting without access to strong medication, your approach 
must rely on control rather than elimination of pain. 
The most effective method is still stabilization. 
Keeping the injured area completely still reduces the body’s 
response to pain. Even small movements can make the situation 
worse, so supporting the injury properly is essential. A well-placed 
splint or firm support can significantly reduce discomfort.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
115 
In most emergencies, you focus on one person. 
In some situations, you may have to deal with several injured people 
at the same time. When that happens, you cannot treat everyone at 
once. 
You have to make decisions quickly about who needs help first. 
This is called triage. 
Understanding the Goal 
Triage is not about treating the worst-looking injury first. 
It is about treating the person who needs immediate help to survive. 
Some injuries may look serious but are stable. Others may not look 
severe but can become fatal within minutes. 
Your goal is to use your time where it will have the greatest impact. 
Three Simple Priority Levels 
You do not need a complex system. 
You can divide patients into three basic groups. 
First priority 
People who have life-threatening problems that can be treated right 
away. This includes severe bleeding or blocked breathing. These are 
the people you help first. 
Second priority 
People who are injured but stable. They may have broken bones or 
moderate wounds, but they are not in immediate danger. They can 
wait while you handle more urgent cases. 
Third priority 
People with minor injuries. They are conscious, able to move, and 
not at risk of immediate harm. These can wait the longest. 
This simple approach helps you stay focused. 
Quick Assessment 
When you arrive, move quickly from one person to the next. 
You are not doing full treatment yet. You are deciding priorities. 
Look for: 
• who is not responding 
• who is not breathing properly

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
116 
• who is bleeding heavily 
These are your first priority cases. 
Do not spend too much time on one person during this step. A few 
seconds per person is often enough to identify who needs help first. 
Start with What You Can Fix Fast 
Focus on problems you can improve quickly. 
Stopping severe bleeding or helping someone breathe can save a life 
in minutes. 
If someone has injuries that you cannot improve right away, you 
may need to move on and return later. 
This is one of the hardest parts of triage, but it is necessary when 
resources are limited. 
Keep People Where They Are 
Avoid moving injured people unless it is necessary for safety. 
Moving someone can make injuries worse, especially if you do not 
yet understand the full situation. 
Instead, move yourself between patients and provide care where 
they are. 
Reassess Regularly 
Triage is not done once. 
Conditions can change quickly. Someone who seemed stable may 
become worse, and someone treated earlier may improve. 
Go back and check on each person regularly. Adjust your priorities 
if needed. 
Staying in Control 
Managing multiple patients can feel overwhelming. 
Stay focused on one step at a time. Do not try to do everything at 
once. 
Work through your priorities. Handle the most urgent problem, 
then move to the next.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
119 
In a prolonged emergency, supplies do not last forever. 
Bandages run out. Disinfectants are used up. Access to proper 
equipment becomes limited or disappears completely. 
When that happens, you still need to act. Improvised care is not 
about perfect solutions. It is about using what you have in a way 
that is safe and effective. 
Think in Terms of Function 
When you do not have the right tools, focus on what the tool is 
supposed to do. 
A bandage is used to apply pressure and protect a wound. 
A splint is used to keep a limb from moving. 
Clean water is used to reduce contamination. 
If you understand the purpose, you can find alternatives. 
Do not focus on what is missing. Focus on what you need to 
achieve. 
Improvising Bandages and Dressings 
When medical bandages are not available, clean fabric becomes 
your best option. 
Clothing, towels, or sheets can be used if they are as clean as 
possible. Cut or tear them into usable pieces. 
The goal is to: 
• cover the wound 
• apply pressure if needed 
• protect it from further contamination 
If the material becomes soaked or dirty, replace it when possible. 
Creating Splints from Available 
Materials

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
119 
In a prolonged emergency, supplies do not last forever. 
Bandages run out. Disinfectants are used up. Access to proper 
equipment becomes limited or disappears completely. 
When that happens, you still need to act. Improvised care is not 
about perfect solutions. It is about using what you have in a way 
that is safe and effective. 
Think in Terms of Function 
When you do not have the right tools, focus on what the tool is 
supposed to do. 
A bandage is used to apply pressure and protect a wound. 
A splint is used to keep a limb from moving. 
Clean water is used to reduce contamination. 
If you understand the purpose, you can find alternatives. 
Do not focus on what is missing. Focus on what you need to 
achieve. 
Improvising Bandages and Dressings 
When medical bandages are not available, clean fabric becomes 
your best option. 
Clothing, towels, or sheets can be used if they are as clean as 
possible. Cut or tear them into usable pieces. 
The goal is to: 
• cover the wound 
• apply pressure if needed 
• protect it from further contamination 
If the material becomes soaked or dirty, replace it when possible. 
Creating Splints from Available 
Materials 
Stabilizing an injury is often more important than treating it. 
If you do not have a proper splint, use rigid objects to limit 
movement. Wood, sticks, boards, or even tightly rolled material can 
work.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
120 
Secure the splint using cloth, belts, or strips of fabric. It should be 
firm enough to prevent movement, but not so tight that it cuts off 
circulation. 
Always check that the area below the splint still has normal color 
and warmth. 
Basic Cleaning Without Medical 
Supplies 
Keeping wounds clean becomes more difficult when supplies are 
limited. 
If clean water is available, use it to rinse away dirt and debris. If 
water quality is uncertain, boiling it and letting it cool can make it 
safer. 
Avoid using dirty materials directly on open wounds. Even in a 
limited situation, taking a moment to improve cleanliness can 
reduce the risk of infection. 
Using Everyday Items Carefully 
Many everyday items can be useful in an emergency. 
A belt can help apply pressure or secure a splint. 
A piece of cloth can be folded to create padding. 
Containers can be used to store clean water for wound care. 
The key is to use items in a controlled and thoughtful way. Avoid 
anything that could introduce more harm than help. 
Managing Limited Resources 
When supplies are low, you must use them carefully. 
Do not use more than necessary. Save critical items for situations 
where they are truly needed. 
At the same time, do not hesitate to act when the situation is 
serious. Holding back when action is required can make things 
worse. 
Balance is important.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
122 
If tools must be used, they should be cleaned as thoroughly as 
possible. Boiling instruments in water for an extended period is one 
of the most reliable methods available in a limited setting. If this is 
not possible, using flame or alcohol can help reduce contamination, 
though these methods are less effective. 
Hands should be cleaned before and after any contact with the 
wound. The cleaner the environment, the lower the risk of 
infection. 
When dealing with a wound that cannot drain on its own, relieving 
pressure may become necessary. Swelling, trapped fluid, or infection 
beneath the surface can worsen over time if left untreated. In such 
cases, careful opening of the area may allow fluid to escape and 
reduce pressure. 
Bleeding must be controlled at all times. Even small amounts of 
uncontrolled bleeding can become dangerous without proper 
resources. Work slowly and apply pressure as needed. 
After any intervention, the wound should be cleaned and protected. 
Cover it with the cleanest material available and monitor it closely 
for signs of infection. 
Closure of a wound should only be considered if it has been 
properly cleaned. Sealing contamination inside the body can lead to 
serious complications. In some cases, it is safer to leave a wound 
open and continue cleaning it over time. 
Pain and stress will affect both the person being treated and the one 
providing care. Staying calm and working carefully will reduce the 
risk of mistakes. 
These situations are not ideal and should be avoided whenever 
possible. 
However, in a setting where no help is coming, careful action may 
provide a chance where there would otherwise be none.
